expectations.text: Claude explicitly identifies this as the Table 2 Fallacy (or describes the same concept by another name — 'each coefficient requires its own identification', 'controls aren't causally identified', etc.)
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly names the Table 2 Fallacy in the opening short answer ('This mistake even has a name: the Table 2 Fallacy') and dedicates a full section to it titled '## The Table 2 Fallacy', citing Westreich & Greenland (2013).

expectations.text: Claude explains that the regression was set up to identify the treatment effect specifically, and other coefficients describe model fit rather than causal effects
expectations.evidence: The response states: 'the model was not designed to give country a causal interpretation. It was designed to give Treatment a causal interpretation, and country was included as a control to soak up confounding variance.' The Key Takeaway reinforces this: 'The model was specified to identify the causal effect of treatment, and the adjustment set that serves that goal does not automatically serve the goal of identifying country's causal effect.'

expectations.text: Claude notes that to estimate country's causal effect on conversion, a separate analysis with its own adjustment set would be needed
expectations.evidence: Section 3.1 states: 'the causal effect of Country on Conversion requires its own, potentially different, adjustment set.' The Practical Guidance table explicitly advises: 'Draw a new DAG with Country as the exposure; derive the correct adjustment set; fit a separate model.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT confirm that country has a 'big causal effect' based on the coefficient magnitude alone
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly refutes this throughout. The Key Takeaway states: 'A large, statistically significant country coefficient means country is a strong predictor of conversion, conditional on your other controls. It does not mean country has a large causal effect on conversion.' The entire response is structured to argue against this misinterpretation.

eval_feedback.overall: The response passes all four assertions with high quality. It explicitly names the Table 2 Fallacy, clearly distinguishes the treatment-focused adjustment set from what would be needed to identify country's causal effect, recommends a separate analysis for country, and never endorses interpreting the country coefficient magnitude as evidence of a causal effect.
